en: The Sūtra on the Dharma-Perception of Dhyāna Practice, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Buddha...
The bhikṣus received the instruction and listened to the Buddha.

If, for even the duration of a finger-snap, one contemplates the perception of death and reflects that all who possess a body must die, this constitutes the practice of dhyāna through diligent application; it is acting in accordance with the Buddha's teaching, and is not like the foolish consumption of the alms offered by the people of a kingdom—how much more so for those who practice extensively!"

To state the essentials: if one contemplates the perception of impurity, the perception of the loathsomeness of food, the perception that there is no pleasure in any world, the perception of impermanence, the perception that what is impermanent is suffering, the perception that what is suffering is not-self, the perception that what is not-self is empty, the perception of relinquishment, the perception of the removal of lust, the perception of cessation, and the perception of non-self;

The perception that the body, upon death, is devoured by worms; the perception of flowing blood; the perception of bloating; the perception of bluish decay; the perception of putrefaction and a rancid stench; the perception of hair falling out and flesh wasting away; the perception of all bonds being severed; the perception of the separation of bones and joints; the perception of the bones changing color—becoming reddish-white, withered black, and like the color of a pigeon; the perception of the bones crumbling into ash; the perception that there is no place of refuge in the world; the perception that there is nothing stable in the world; the perception that the world is characterized by separation; the perception that the world is shrouded in darkness; the perception that the world is unbearable; the perception that the world is a wasteful expenditure and useless; the perception that the world is subject to calamities and is something to be weary of and loathe; and the perception that all worlds ultimately return to *nirvāṇa*.

“Monks, if for even the duration of a finger-snap one contemplates these matters regarding these perceptions, it constitutes diligent practice and is an offering to the Buddha’s teaching; it is not the foolish consumption of others’ alms—how much more so if one can practice them extensively!”
"Therefore, you should mindfully cultivate the perception of the Dharma.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, they all received them with joy.
*The Sūtra on Cultivating the Perception of the Dharma through Meditation*.
